channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Why a Do-Nothing Congress could be great for markets | E2359
gist: A post-midterm VC roundtable (Jason Calacanis, DA Wallik, Elana Gold, Tomas of Theory Ventures) argues a Democratic House+Senate sweep makes data centers and AV politically toxic but reduces Trump-driven macro uncertainty, while a narrowing M&A window, GPU scarcity (Blackwell rental up ~120% to ~$13/hr) and possible AI rationing in 2027 reshape tech. They also dissect Sequoia's restructuring (scouts/Arc/London closed, $10B raised), 'alicorn' capital-efficient startups, the SPV broker boom, and tokenized perps (Hyperliquid) as an end-run around private-market access rules.

themes.theme: Midterm blue wave: politics of AI and data centers

insights.claim: With Democrats taking both the House and Senate, the panel expects divided government to produce gridlock that markets may welcome because it limits Trump-driven chaos such as new wars or tariff shocks.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: A do-nothing Congress may compress macro uncertainty premia even if it slows pro-tech policy.
insights.quote: So I think divided government, even if it means sclerosis, even if it means that nothing gets done in DC, what it does mean is that nothing crazy is likely to happen.

insights.claim: DA Wallik argues the past year's rise in long-term interest rates has been driven more by policy uncertainty and fiscal unsustainability than by AI-related borrowing crowding out other credit.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: If uncertainty falls under divided government, long rates could ease without any change in AI capex.
insights.quote: what we've seen happen in long-term interest rates over the past like, you know, year has been much more about uncertainty and fiscal unsustainability than it has been about crowding out with AI borrowing

insights.claim: Markets were expected to fall 2-4% overnight after the election but rallied instead, which the panel attributes to hopes the war ends and oil-price chaos subsides.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Market read the blue wave as de-risking geopolitics/energy rather than as anti-tech.

insights.claim: An NBC exit poll found 56% of voters called AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their vote, and Democrats spent over $100M on ads tying Republicans to big tech and data centers.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Data-center siting is now a mass-electorate issue, raising permitting and political risk for the buildout trade.
insights.quote: found 56% of voters called AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their vote

insights.claim: Anti-data-center rhetoric is likely to become a bipartisan political winner because defending AI against job-loss fears requires a complicated, counterintuitive argument.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Data-center opposition may persist regardless of which party holds power, a structural headwind to the buildout.

insights.claim: Elana Gold expects data-center buildout to become a state-by-state regulatory fight, but power scarcity remains the binding constraint, driving startup opportunity in nuclear and lower-power chips.
insights.speaker: Elana Gold
insights.so_what: Regulatory friction on data centers strengthens the case for power-efficiency and alternative-power startups.
insights.quote: maybe we can't build out as much data centers, but maybe we're going to build chips that don't require as much power

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis sees a nonzero chance of an anti-self-driving wave spreading across the US, especially from the Northeast, as politicians try to protect driving jobs.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Robotaxi rollouts face rising political/regulatory risk in a jobs-focused political climate.
insights.quote: I think there's a a nonzero chance that we're going to see a wave of anti-self-driving go across the country

insights.claim: DA Wallik frames the election as an intergenerational revolt: older equity owners capture gains from Uber, Tesla, SpaceX and data centers while young gig workers face job threats and unaffordable housing, with Social Security's trust fund insolvent in 2032.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Wealth concentration in equity holders is fueling political backlash against tech; expect policy aimed at young voters.
insights.quote: the intergenerational war is the true winter that is coming.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis argues sentiment will turn when everyday Americans use AI agents that deliver concrete savings, and that Meta's free trades-training program and data-center landing pages are early reputation-repair efforts.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Consumer-agent adoption is the lever that could flip AI's political narrative.

insights.claim: DA Wallik notes the costliest parts of household budgets (rent, healthcare, school, childcare, cars) are physical and largely policy-bound, so AI's biggest help may be making voters and politics smarter rather than directly cutting those costs.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Limits the near-term ability of AI to relieve the cost-of-living anger driving the backlash.

insights.claim: Tomas argues that because HSR/FTC/DOJ reviews take about 18 months, large acquisitions must be executed by roughly June-July 2027 to close before a potential Democratic administration in 2029.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Expect a rush of large tech deals announced in H1 2027.

insights.claim: For the largest tech deals, Chinese regulatory approval rather than US approval is often the long pole, and the EU's merger posture has not changed.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Cross-border megadeals carry geopolitical approval risk independent of US politics.
insights.quote: The long pole in the tent there is actually Chinese approval rather than American approval.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis warns that 2027 may be the last year to get big deals done, followed by potentially five years of little M&A as under Lina Khan.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Startup exit paths via acquisition could narrow sharply after 2027.
insights.quote: 2027 is the last year to get a big deal done and then you could be looking at five years of no more uh you know M&A

themes.theme: Compute scarcity, pricing and AI margins

insights.claim: Tomas says hourly rental cost for state-of-the-art Blackwell 300 GPUs rose about 120%, from roughly $5 to $13, over the past six months.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: GPU rental pricing is signaling acute compute scarcity, bullish for neoclouds and compute owners.
insights.quote: you've seen GPU costs go up uh 120% from about five bucks to about 13 bucks in the last six months.

insights.claim: Tomas predicts there will not be enough AI compute in 2027, leading to AI being bought like internet bandwidth, rationed by volume and speed rather than all-you-can-eat.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Expect tiered/metered AI pricing and pressure on unlimited plans.
insights.quote: we will start to buy AI the way that we buy internet.

insights.claim: Tomas expects roughly 81 gigawatts of capacity next year with about 60% devoted to model training, leaving limited inference even as Vera Rubin chips double productivity and demand grows faster than 200% per year.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Training's share of compute is a key swing factor for inference availability and pricing.

insights.claim: According to the head of Google data centers as cited by Tomas, intelligence per watt is doubling year-over-year, with an overall 400x cost reduction, yet supply remains finite.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Efficiency gains are being outrun by demand, so scarcity persists.
insights.quote: we're seeing a doubling in intelligence per watt year-over-year.

insights.claim: Compute scarcity will make bespoke vibe-coded custom apps too expensive for most, driving a resurgence of the packaged application layer.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Contrary to 'SaaS is dead', constrained inference could favor app-layer software vendors.
insights.quote: I think we'll ultimately see a pretty big resurgence at the app layer

insights.claim: Tomas cites Anthropic's S1 showing roughly 81-82% gross margin versus about 71% for public software companies, alongside price wars such as OpenAI cutting prices 50% then 80% and open-source models 80-85% cheaper.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Frontier labs currently out-earn SaaS on gross margin despite deflationary pressure.
insights.quote: you can look at the anthropic S1 approximately 81 82% gross margin compared to a publicly traded software company of about 71

insights.claim: Tomas frames frontier labs like pharma with a 41-day instead of 17-year exclusivity window, so they need high margins in that window to fund the next model.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: High lab margins are a funding necessity, not necessarily monopoly rents.
insights.quote: If I'm a state-of-the-art AI lab, I have 41 days because in 41 days, someone else is coming out with another soda model

insights.claim: DA Wallik questions whether the Silicon Valley 'everyone wins' thesis, with memory makers, Nvidia, neoclouds and labs all earning ~80% margins, is sustainable, noting Micron trades at about 4.5x and SK Hynix about 2.8x forward P/E.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Memory stocks' low multiples imply the market doubts durable margins.
insights.quote: Micron's trading at a forward P of 4 1/2. Hinck's trading at a forward P of 2.8.

insights.claim: Tomas would not load up on hardware stocks because GPUs are sitting in warehouses for lack of electricity, so Nvidia bookings could plateau and trigger a seismic shock.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Power, not chip demand, may cap hardware revenue growth; a key risk for semis.
insights.quote: their GPUs lying in warehouses. We don't have enough electricity to light them up.

insights.claim: Tomas argues 70-80% gross margins for AI firms can be sustainable, citing AWS's 35-36% operating margins even while selling commodity compute.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Commodity-like compute can still sustain healthy profits with competition.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says his firm spends about $40,000 on AI tools and estimates roughly $2 million in value, having built three internal software platforms in months without developers.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: AI tooling may be massively underpriced relative to value, implying pricing power for vendors.

insights.claim: Local inference will boom in a GPU-limited 2027; Tomas cites a Stanford study that 90% of non-coder AI work can run on a local model and Ollama's roughly 10 million users.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Demand shifts toward high-end local hardware and hybrid local/cloud inference.

insights.claim: Canva cut about 20-22% of staff, which Jason Calacanis attributes to AI compressing what customers pay for, suggesting AI-wrapper software margins will be squeezed.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Software firms dependent on third-party inference face margin and headcount pressure.

insights.claim: SpaceX's data-center build (Colossus 2 four times larger than Colossus 1) is so lucrative that Elon Musk is shifting rocket engineers to general-contracting work.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Data-center construction speed is now a strategic priority even for frontier engineering firms.

insights.claim: DA Wallik suggests the mandate to shift to self-driving may come from insurers, with car insurance eventually looking like title insurance with very low payout rates.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Possible convergence of AV operators and insurance; incumbent auto insurers face disruption.
insights.quote: I think maybe car insurance ultimately ends up looking like title insurance

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis predicts being anti-AI will become an increasingly losing political position as consumers get huge value from it, e.g., Zipline drone delivery.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Tangible consumer AI/robotics wins could reverse the backlash.

insights.claim: Sequoia is closing its London office, sunsetting the Arc accelerator and the Scout program, simplifying Sequoia Capital Fund, merging early and growth stages, ending the Monday partner meeting, and has raised $10B in new funds.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The top VC brand is simplifying and scaling up rather than expanding early-stage programs.

insights.claim: Tomas argues unifying early and growth funds makes sense because a 'seed' round can now be $5M, $50M or $500M, as neolab research teams may need $300-500M to prove an idea.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Stage-based fund structures are obsolete for AI; mega-funds gain an edge on frontier research startups.

insights.claim: DA Wallik argues a $10B venture fund can hardly deliver the outsized returns that define venture, creating an opening for small agile funds embedded in young founders' networks.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Small early-stage funds may be the better LP product as mega-funds become asset managers.
insights.quote: very very hard to do that with $10 billion no matter what you're doing right, no matter how smart you are.

insights.claim: DA Wallik predicts venture firms will try to go public, as Blackstone, Ares and Apollo did, so founders can monetize their equity, fundamentally changing these businesses.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Watch for VC firm IPOs or permanent-capital vehicles.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis describes 'alicorns': AI-native startups with two or three people reaching $10-100K monthly revenue that fly over funding rounds because they are profitable, making good VC entry prices harder.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: VC returns shift toward either very early or crossover-like late-stage access.

insights.claim: a16z's Speedrun invests $500K at $5M with an option for another $500K at $20M, targeting 10-12% ownership.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Accelerator terms are a competitive lever as Sequoia exits the accelerator game.

insights.claim: Elana Gold observes founders increasingly offering uncapped SAFEs with 10-15% discounts and LPs accepting them, which may be a top-of-market signal.
insights.speaker: Elana Gold
insights.so_what: Loosening investor terms are a frothiness indicator in private markets.

themes.theme: Private market access, secondaries and tokenization

insights.claim: DA Wallik calls the SPV/secondary boom 'freelance investment banking' by unlicensed brokers, a symptom of public-market failure where growth companies stay private too long and retail gets the dregs.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Supports policy pressure for earlier IPOs and scrutiny of SPV fee chains.
insights.quote: there's this new industry of freelance investment banking where people's, you know, they're not investors, they're they're brokers

insights.claim: DA Wallik argues asset managers are pushing private equity and private credit into 401(k)s because ETFs commoditized active public equity, removing their fee pool.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Retail private-asset products are fee-driven; be skeptical of the investor benefit.
insights.quote: ETFs have commoditized active public equity management. All the money is gone from that.

insights.claim: Tomas attributes fewer public companies to high IPO costs (about $25M for a $100M-revenue company a decade ago vs ~$0.5M privately) and the JOBS Act raising shareholder-count limits.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Regulatory relaxation, not just capital abundance, explains the shrinking public market.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis advocates letting non-accredited people qualify via a course, and expects Democrats to revert to a protectionist stance on accredited-investor reform.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Accredited-investor liberalization may stall under the new Congress.

insights.claim: Tokenized assets and perpetual futures on platforms like Hyperliquid could conceptually supersede the regulated securities market by letting anyone bet on private company valuations, with pre-IPO price discovery on names like Anthropic.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Synthetic markets are an emerging retail end-run around private-market access rules, likely to draw US regulation.
insights.quote: It's permissionless. I don't need some SPV hustler to get me into Palunteer

insights.claim: Tomas says tokenization of equities and debt is growing faster than AI and that the largest banks are pushing aggressively into tokenizing public and private assets.
insights.speaker: Tomas
insights.so_what: Tokenization infrastructure is a large near-term market opportunity.
insights.quote: It's growing faster than AI. It's the fastest growing technology market in the world.

insights.claim: DA Wallik links leveraged ETFs and high-leverage perps to envy-driven risk-taking among workers told they have three years to make all their money before AI freezes the economic hierarchy.
insights.speaker: DA Wallik
insights.so_what: Retail speculative leverage is a social-stress indicator with retirement-risk consequences.
insights.quote: the world's not run by greed, it's run by envy.
